newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Delors says euro a priority for the left.
newsitem.headline: France's Delors says euro a priority for the left.

text.p: Former European Commission chief Jacques Delors has said the French left would make the single European currency its priority if it came to power in Sunday's parliamentary election runoff.

"I have no doubt about this," Delors, a former French Socialist finance minister, told the weekly Le Nouvel Observateur in an interview published on Tuesday after the left upset the ruling right in last Sunday's first-round vote.
"Respecting the (1999) deadline for European economic and monetary union appears as an absolute obligation," he said.
Socialist plans to re-focus economic policy on creating jobs did not run contrary to the spirit of the Maastricht Treaty even if it meant slightly relaxing the budget criteria, Delors said.
He said the spirit of Maastricht was a commitment to lasting financial health rather than toeing the three percent limit on budget deficit to the last decimal.

"I was in Germany two weeks ago. I saw that the three per cent blackmail was on the way out," he said. "Historians will see as paltry the financial solutions that will be found to respect (the 1999 deadline) given the importance of what is at stake."

Delors, who is seen in opinion polls as the voters' favourite to become French premier should the left win Sunday's election runoff, did not say whether he would seek a government job. He dropped out of public life two years ago when he declined to contest the presidential election.

Delors said the conservatives had failed to convince voters that they could adapt the country to world changes, and the left was now better placed to face the challenge of globalisation because it could win social backing for reforms.
"Only the left can today prove to the French people that adaptation to globalisation and technical progress is not contrary to social progress," he said.

But he said the left could not ignore the current challenges of heightened competition between industrialised countries and the calling into question of hugely costly social protection systems as the population grows older.

"We must explain to the French people that the ship France must leave port and face the high seas because this is the only way they can retain their living standards and regain influence in Europe and the world," he said.
